newsitem.title: ALBANIA: Albania to approve U.N. force amid outrage with Italy.
newsitem.headline: Albania to approve U.N. force amid outrage with Italy.

text.p: Albania is due to give final approval on Sunday to an Italian-led force to protect aid supplies to the anarchic Balkan state despite its anger with Rome over the sinking of an illegal Albanian refugee boat.

Albania's parliament meets at 11 a.m. (0900 GMT) on the U.N.-approved plan to send a force, of police or troops, to protect food and medical supplies to Europe's poorest nation, racked by armed insurrection and banditry.
But Albanian leaders left little doubt that the People's Assembly would back the plan, even though the sinking of a crammed refugee boat in the Adriatic on Friday badly jolted ties with Italy.
Italy said at least four people drowned after the Russian-built harbour patrol craft sank in a collision with a Italian corvette enforcing orders to turn back refugees from Albania.
But some of the 34 survivors of the sinking said that as many as 100 people had been on board and were feared drowned.

Albania's right-wing President Sali Berisha, who has repeatedly called for a U.N.-approved security force, urged the Italian authorities "to investigate and take necessary measures to ensure that such events are not repeated."
Prime Minister Bashkim Fino also demanded an Italian investigation and said the "tragedy should have been avoided."
But he also voiced conviction that it "would not question the good and close Albanian-Italian relations and the coming bilateral cooperation to overcome the grave situation in Albania."
"The international military force will be a basic element in the efforts the Albanians are making to overcome the deep crisis which is ruining the country," he added.
Italy estimates that 2,500 security personnel should be sent to Albania, with a similar number in reserve, to counter the civil chaos that has claimed scores of lives there.

Italy has become Albania's closest economic partner since the Cold War. And few Albanians bear grudges over Rome's two occupations this century, in 1914 and 1939, reckoning that communism under late dictator Enver Hoxha was far worse.
Hoxha, who ruled for 40 years until his death in 1985, turned Albania into a hermit state that turned its back even on Moscow and Beijing.
Italian Prime Minister Romano Prodi said the sinking added urgency to Italy's planned international security mission to Albania.
About 13,000 Albanian refugees have reached Italy and Prodi said the navy would continue to patrol the southern Adriatic to prevent more arriving.

Italy sees the relief operation as essential to stabilising the country, where anger over the collapse of popular savings schemes exploded into civil violence in mid-March, and paving the way for national elections in June.

The force is due to secure Tirana's international airport along with the ports of Durres and Vlore and international aid convoys. Other countries expected to participate are Greece, France, Spain, Portugal and perhaps Turkey and Romania.
But some relief groups, including the neutral Red Cross, question whether the force will actually help in distributing aid.

A Red Cross truck delivered aid through southern Albania without incident this week.. "Our operation has gone without problems," said Darcy Christen, the head of the mission. "I wouldn't be too happy to have them (a force) with us."
